questions.prompt: Rows share created_at timestamps. Which ordering gives pagination a deterministic tie-breaker when id is unique?

choices.text: ORDER BY a constant expression for every row.
ORDER BY created_at, id.
ORDER BY created_at alone.
No ORDER BY because an index fixes output order.

questions.explanation: A unique final key resolves timestamp ties. Physical or index order is not a substitute for a requested total ordering.

sources.title: LIMIT and OFFSET
sources.claim: LIMIT without a uniquely constraining ORDER BY can return unpredictable subsets; OFFSET skips rows that still must be computed, and differing LIMIT/OFFSET values can lead to different plans.

questions.prompt: A SELECT uses LIMIT 20 without ORDER BY. What output order should its API promise?

choices.text: No deterministic order without an appropriate ORDER BY.
A stable order whenever the previous page was cached.
The same insertion order across every execution plan.
The primary-key order even when it was not requested.

questions.explanation: SQL does not promise a stable subset for unordered LIMIT. Define a unique order before promising pagination semantics.

sources.title: LIMIT and OFFSET
sources.claim: LIMIT without a uniquely constraining ORDER BY can return unpredictable subsets; OFFSET skips rows that still must be computed, and differing LIMIT/OFFSET values can lead to different plans.

questions.prompt: Why can a very large OFFSET make a query expensive even when LIMIT is small?

choices.text: Skipped rows still must be computed before returning the requested rows.
LIMIT causes skipped rows to be processed only when the API fetches the previous page.
OFFSET is expensive only because it changes the stored ordering of table rows.
OFFSET can seek directly to a numeric position without computing any preceding rows.

questions.explanation: The database must compute and skip the preceding rows. A small result size alone does not imply small work.

sources.title: LIMIT and OFFSET
sources.claim: LIMIT without a uniquely constraining ORDER BY can return unpredictable subsets; OFFSET skips rows that still must be computed, and differing LIMIT/OFFSET values can lead to different plans.

questions.prompt: A newly inserted row sorts before page one after that page is read. What can happen to page two obtained by OFFSET?

choices.text: Every previously returned row is automatically removed from the dataset.
OFFSET retains a snapshot cursor from the earlier HTTP request.
A boundary row can repeat because its numerical position shifted.
The unique ORDER BY prevents all shifts caused by new insertions.

questions.explanation: OFFSET identifies positions in the current result. An insertion before the boundary can shift an already seen row into the next page.

sources.title: LIMIT and OFFSET
sources.claim: OFFSET skips a numerical count of ordered rows; each independently evaluated query uses its current result rather than a retained cursor.

questions.prompt: An ascending page uses non-NULL (created_at, id). Which continuation predicate matches a cursor (:time, :id)?

choices.text: created_at = :time AND id = :id.
(created_at, id) > (:time, :id).
id < :id regardless of the created_at ordering.
created_at >= :time without an id condition.

questions.explanation: The lexicographic greater-than boundary matches ascending timestamp then id ordering and excludes the cursor row.

sources.title: Row and Array Comparisons
sources.claim: Row comparisons compare corresponding fields left-to-right until unequal non-NULL fields determine ordering; composite comparisons can express an ascending keyset boundary when keys are non-NULL.

questions.prompt: Two independent Read Committed requests use keyset pagination. What does the cursor alone guarantee?

choices.text: A continuation boundary, without guaranteeing one fixed snapshot.
Updates to ordering keys can never affect later page membership.
All later requests reuse the first transaction automatically.
The entire dataset is frozen at the first request time.

questions.explanation: A cursor expresses where to continue in an ordering. Snapshot consistency requires an additional transaction or application design.

sources.title: Transaction Isolation
sources.claim: Read Committed obtains new statement snapshots, while Repeatable Read maintains a transaction snapshot; a keyset predicate alone does not create a fixed dataset snapshot across requests.

questions.prompt: Which ordering claims support deterministic pages? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A primary key guarantees SELECT output order without ORDER BY.
Timestamp ties need a unique tie-breaker for a total order.
Physical row order remains contractual after changing the query plan.
ORDER BY created_at, id resolves ties when id is unique.
LIMIT alone determines which rows are logically first.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: uniqueness does not request sorting. B: Correct: otherwise ties leave relative order unresolved. C: Incorrect: physical order is not an output guarantee. D: Correct: the pair gives distinct ordered positions. E: Incorrect: the ordering must be defined.

sources.title: LIMIT and OFFSET
sources.claim: LIMIT requires ORDER BY that constrains rows into a unique order for predictable subsets.

questions.prompt: Which OFFSET considerations are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Skipped rows can still contribute query work.
A small LIMIT guarantees that few rows need to be computed.
Changing data can shift which rows occupy a later offset.
An insertion before the boundary cannot change numeric row positions.
OFFSET retains the first request snapshot automatically.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: PostgreSQL computes rows it skips. B: Incorrect: a large offset can require substantial skipped work. C: Correct: offsets are positions in the evaluated result. D: Incorrect: earlier insertions can shift later positions. E: Incorrect: it contains no snapshot identity.

sources.title: LIMIT and OFFSET
sources.claim: OFFSET rows must still be computed and LIMIT/OFFSET operate on the ordered result evaluated for that query.

questions.prompt: Which composite keyset decisions match ascending non-NULL (created_at, id) ordering? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Store both ordered key values in the continuation cursor.
Use the same key ordering in the predicate and ORDER BY.
Compare only the timestamp even when many rows share it.
Use greater-than-or-equal to include the cursor row on the next page.
Use a greater-than row comparison against the cursor pair.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: both values locate the position. B: Correct: mismatched ordering defines a different boundary. C: Incorrect: timestamp ties need the id boundary. D: Incorrect: a strict boundary excludes the already returned row. E: Correct: lexicographic comparison matches ascending continuation.

sources.title: Row and Array Comparisons
sources.claim: Row comparisons use left-to-right lexicographic ordering; strict greater-than on non-NULL key pairs excludes the cursor and selects later ordered pairs.

questions.prompt: Which cross-page consistency claims are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A continuation boundary and a fixed snapshot are separate requirements.
A keyset cursor automatically opens one transaction spanning all requests.
Keyset boundaries alone prohibit later updates to ordering keys.
A Repeatable Read transaction can provide a stable view for its reads.
Independent Read Committed queries can see different committed states.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: ordered continuation alone is not temporal consistency. B: Incorrect: cursor data does not manage transaction lifetime. C: Incorrect: a cursor does not lock or freeze ordering values. D: Correct: reads share that transaction snapshot. E: Correct: their statement snapshots may differ.
